extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory, historians, and policymakers studying American municipal and democratic institutions
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts normative criteria and institutional features used to evaluate municipal government and the broader political consequences of social equality in 19th-century America (township organization, popular sovereignty, electoral extension).

rubrics_metrics.name: Social equality as determinant of political outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: When men are more equal in fortune and intellect than elsewhere, this social equality will inevitably find its way into the political world and shape political results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text explains that equality in social conditions predisposes a nation toward two possible political consequences (sovereignty of all or absolute power of one) and that political institutions must be analyzed in light of prevailing social equality. Use this criterion to evaluate how strongly social homogeneity influences political structures and behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of the sovereignty of the people in laws and customs
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of the sovereignty of the people is 'recognised by the customs and proclaimed by the laws' in America; it spreads freely and appears in every possible form according to exigency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether popular sovereignty is not merely rhetorical but embedded in both legal frameworks and everyday customs—visible in elective mechanisms, popular control of legislators, and administrative accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent and trajectory of elective qualification (expansion toward universal suffrage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes to the elective qualification tend to continue until universal suffrage is reached; 'concession follows concession' and no stop can be made short of universal suffrage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the breadth of the electoral franchise, historical tendencies for extension, and whether incremental expansions make further extension likely. Use to predict democratization pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Municipal institutions as the foundation of liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: Municipal institutions are to liberty what primary schools are to science: they bring liberty within the people's reach and teach citizens how to use and enjoy it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use strength and prevalence of local municipal bodies (townships, town-meetings) as a measure of the practical health of liberty and civic education in a polity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Township sovereignty in local matters vs. state authority in other matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The township of New England is sovereign in that which concerns itself alone, but is subject to the State in all other matters; there exists a bond between township and state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the degree of local autonomy retained by municipalities: what matters they control exclusively versus those reserved for state/federal authority, and whether this balance is respected in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct popular governance via town-meeting (absence of representative corporation)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the township, the system of representation is not adopted; there is no corporation — the body of electors directs its magistrates and acts directly through town-meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the presence and functioning of direct-democratic mechanisms (town-meetings), the frequency and scope of direct decisions, and the degree to which officials act as executors of explicit popular mandates rather than autonomous administrators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selectmen as principal administrative agents with legally defined obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: The selectmen manage a large proportion of administrative power, are obliged by state law to perform duties (e.g., draw up the list of electors), and may be guilty of misdemeanor if they omit required functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate local executive accountability by checking whether principal municipal officers have legally enforced duties, the clarity of those duties, procedures (e.g., calling town meetings), and sanctions for neglect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth, compulsory nature, and remuneration of municipal offices
rubrics_metrics.description: There are nineteen principal offices in a township; every inhabitant may be compelled (on pain of fine) to undertake these functions, and most offices are paid so that poorer citizens can serve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the scope and compulsory rotation of municipal duties and the system of per-service remuneration to judge inclusiveness, civic burden-sharing, and accessibility of local governance to all socioeconomic classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate size/scale of the township for effective self-governance
rubrics_metrics.description: The township of New England has an average population of 2,000 (2–3 thousand), so that interests are unlikely to conflict and persons capable of conducting affairs exist among citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a local unit's population and scale permit effective direct participation and availability of competent municipal actors; use the 2,000–3,000 figure as an illustrative benchmark for effective township governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fragility of municipal freedom and need for cultural/legal consolidation
rubrics_metrics.description: Municipal freedom is rarely created and easily destroyed; it survives only when amalgamated with national laws, manners, peculiar circumstances, and time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the durability of local autonomy by checking whether municipal practices are supported by long-standing laws and national customs; be alert to centralized encroachments and absence of public opinion support as signs of fragility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two alternative methods of establishing political equality
rubrics_metrics.description: Only two methods of establishing equality in the political world exist: every citizen must be put in possession of his rights, or rights must be granted to no one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this binary as a conceptual test: does the polity distribute rights broadly to realize popular sovereignty, or does it suppress rights universally (potentially creating despotism)? Evaluate institutions against this dichotomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk that the passion for equality may undermine liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists a depraved taste for equality which impels the weak to lower the powerful to their level and may lead people to 'prefer equality in slavery to inequality with freedom.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether egalitarian impulses are channeled toward preserving liberty or toward leveling that risks tyranny; look for institutional safeguards that prevent equality-focused movements from sacrificing fundamental freedoms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological necessity of examining state-level institutions before the federal
rubrics_metrics.description: To examine the Union before having studied the states would be to adopt a method filled with obstacles; the great political principles took origin and growth in the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For institutional analysis, prioritize detailed study of state and municipal structures (township, county, state) before addressing federal arrangements; interpret federal mechanisms as modifications of prevailing state-level republican principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: American mode of remunerating municipal functionaries (pay per service)
rubrics_metrics.description: The American system is generally not to grant a fixed salary to its functionaries; every service has its price and they are remunerated in proportion to what they have done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate municipal compensation systems for their inclusivity and practicality: per-service payment can enable poorer citizens to serve, but examine whether it creates incentives or inequalities in public service provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast in state–commune relations between France and America (agents vs. locally-supplied officials)
rubrics_metrics.description: In France the Government lends its agents to the commune; in America the reverse occurs—the township supplies its own officers and governs local matters directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this comparative criterion to judge centralization: whether local administration depends on centrally appointed agents or on locally elected/selected officers; prefer locally-supplied administration for stronger municipal independence per the text.
